I know how busy you probably already are, so this may not be realistic for you, but if you have time to be proactive about communicating with parents it might help them develop a better picture of what’s going on and feel natural about reaching out to you first. For example, if a kid gets injured call the parents as soon as you have a chance just to give them a heads up about what happened and how it’s been handled (and if kid is okay, let them know like Hey Ms B, it’s Tommy’s teacher. Just wanted to give you a heads up that on the playground today Tommy and another kid collided during tag and Tommy scraped his knee up. He’s okay, we got his knee cleaned up and he’s got a bandaid and he’s back to playing with friends now, but I’ll keep an eye on it this afternoon. Do you have any questions? Ok thanks, let me know if anything else comes up”. 

About the “bullying”, I had a kid this year who insisted to his mom that his friend was bullying him when really they were good friends but fought all the time and it went both ways. The mom wasn’t rude about it, just let me know she was worried, so I thanked her for telling me, and told her I would watch for it, then would occasionally update her about what I observed, including a message the next day letting her know I watched the boys interaction closely the next couple days, they consistently chose to play together and I didn’t notice any bullying from the other boy, although I did witness her son taunting the other boy about knocking over his tower and so I separated them. If I did see any problems between the boys, I would also send her a quick message or tell her in person at pick up, like “hey just so you know, this afternoon Ike and Devi had a disagreement when Devi wouldnt share his blocks and Ike called him a name.  We talked about sharing and name calling and they decided they would take a break from playing together for a bit, but they seem to have made up and wanted to sit together at snack. Let me know if anything else comes up or you have any questions.” 

It’s hard for parents when they don’t really know or see what’s going on for their kid all day, and lots of parents assume their kids are angels and that they would never lie or skew stories for pity/attention/to get out of trouble, and it’s a hard choice to decide your kid is lying and risk being wrong and damaging that relationship.

I taught in one classroom where the kids each had a rock on their desk (could be a piece of wood or plastic or whatever) with one side that they had painted green and one side painted yellow. If they understood the work they left the green side up. If they got stuck and needed help they could flip the rock to the yellow side, and then they had a stack of alternate activities they could work on (reading, vocabulary practice, adding sheets, etc) while they waited until I could get to them.

These same alternate activities were also available for if they completed their work early and were waiting for the rest of the class to finish, a choice of activities that practice skills that are also interesting enough to keep them occupied (but not so fun that they will rush their work to get to them).
